reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive sterol-storage disorder caused by mutations in the ABCG5 or ABCG8 sterol transporter genes
The defective transporter fails to limit intestinal absorption of plant and shellfish sterols and to promote their biliary excretion, so dietary phytosterols accumulate
Presents with tendon and tuberous xanthomata, often from childhood, sometimes with a normal or only modestly raised total cholesterol
Carries a markedly increased risk of premature atherosclerosis and coronary disease, occasionally with sudden cardiac events in young patients
Haematological features can include haemolytic anaemia with stomatocytes and abnormally large platelets (macrothrombocytopenia)
The biochemical hallmark is grossly raised plasma plant sterols (sitosterol, campesterol) measured by specialised chromatography, which routine cholesterol assays miss

Treatment is a diet low in plant and shellfish sterols combined with ezetimibe and/or bile-acid sequestrants; statins are relatively ineffective and this must be distinguished from familial hypercholesterolaemia
reference.pathophysiology: Sitosterolaemia results from loss of function of the ABCG5/ABCG8 heterodimeric transporter expressed on enterocytes and hepatocytes. Normally this pump exports non-cholesterol sterols back into the gut lumen and into bile, keeping absorption of dietary plant sterols very low. When it is defective, plant sterols such as sitosterol and campesterol, along with cholesterol, are absorbed in excess and poorly excreted, so they accumulate in plasma and tissues. Deposition in tendons and skin causes xanthomata and in arterial walls accelerates atherosclerosis, while incorporation of abnormal sterols into red cell and platelet membranes underlies the haemolysis and macrothrombocytopenia.
additionalDifferentials: Familial hypercholesterolaemia (xanthomata with markedly raised LDL cholesterol)
Other causes of macrothrombocytopenia and haemolytic anaemia
Tangier disease and other rare lipid disorders
additionalInvestigations: Plasma plant sterol quantification (sitosterol and campesterol) by gas chromatography or mass spectrometry
Fasting lipid profile, recognising cholesterol may be only mildly elevated
Full blood count and film for haemolysis, stomatocytes and macrothrombocytopenia
Molecular genetic testing of the ABCG5 and ABCG8 genes
Family screening given the recessive inheritance
redFlags: Premature coronary artery disease or sudden cardiac event in a young patient
Extensive xanthomata in childhood, particularly with normal or near-normal cholesterol
Significant haemolytic anaemia or bleeding from macrothrombocytopenia
Family history of early cardiovascular death
reference.prognosis: With early diagnosis, sterol-restricted diet and sterol-absorption-blocking therapy, plant sterol levels fall, xanthomata regress and cardiovascular risk improves; undiagnosed disease carries a substantial risk of premature atherosclerotic events.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as familial hypercholesterolaemia and relying on statins, which are relatively ineffective
Missing the diagnosis because routine cholesterol assays do not measure plant sterols
Overlooking haematological clues such as haemolysis and large platelets
Underestimating cardiovascular risk when cholesterol appears near normal
Failing to advise dietary restriction of plant and shellfish sterols
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
management: Strict dietary restriction of plant sterols and shellfish sterols, avoiding vegetable oils, nuts, seeds and shellfish, as the cornerstone of treatment
Ezetimibe, an intestinal sterol-absorption inhibitor, as the principal pharmacological therapy to reduce phytosterol absorption
Bile acid sequestrants such as colestyramine as adjunctive sterol-lowering therapy, recognising that statins are of limited value because endogenous cholesterol synthesis is already suppressed
Monitoring of plasma plant sterol levels, lipid profile and regression of xanthomata to guide therapy
Management of the haematological features of haemolytic anaemia and macrothrombocytopenia, which improve with sterol lowering, avoiding misdirected immune therapy or splenectomy
Cardiovascular risk assessment and surveillance for premature atherosclerosis and coronary disease
Genetic counselling and family screening for the autosomal recessive ABCG5 or ABCG8 disorder
